name: Extrinsic incentives bias
statement: People predict that others are driven more by pay and job security, and less by interest and learning, than they report being driven themselves.
meaning: The claim is about prediction, and it has two halves. Asked what moves other people at work, respondents rank pay, benefits and job security higher than those same people rank them for themselves. Asked about interest, learning and worthwhile work, they rank those lower for others than for themselves. DeVoe and Iyengar quote Heath's summary of this: in their lay theories, members of the general population assess others' motives using Theory X, while they assess their own motives using Theory Y. The practical worry is about principals designing deals for agents. Someone who believes staff work only for money will build a scheme around money, and the belief rather than the evidence is doing the designing.

origin.where: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
origin.note: The paper names the bias and reports three laboratory studies and one field study. Its abstract also claims the bias is separable from a self-serving bias and runs counter to the usual actor-observer effect.

evidence: Heath's paper sits behind a paywall at Elsevier and could not be read for this entry. Its abstract, read at PubMed, says people predict that others are more motivated than themselves by extrinsic incentives such as job security and pay, and less motivated by intrinsic ones such as learning new things. The figures usually quoted come at one remove, from DeVoe and Iyengar's description of the paper. On their account Heath found 73% of survey respondents agreeing that large differences in pay were needed to get people to work hard, and 67% agreeing that people would not take extra responsibility at work unless paid extra for it. Those same respondents ranked pay third among aspects of their own jobs, and half of them ranked important work first. In one laboratory study, again on DeVoe and Iyengar's account, participants ranked an extrinsic item most important 22% of the time, while predicting that 32% of classmates, 54% of bank managers and 85% of bank employees would do so.

replication.headline: The self-other gap reappears in North American samples using other methods, and the one large cross-cultural field test finds it absent among Asian managers and reversed among Latin American ones.
replication.detail: DeVoe and Iyengar surveyed 185 Citigroup consumer branch managers and 1,760 of their employees across six countries, with response rates of 86% and 95%. North American managers rated their employees higher on extrinsic than intrinsic motivation, 6.97 against 6.30, F(1, 690) = 10.68, p < .01, partial eta squared .02. North American employees rated themselves the other way, 6.59 intrinsic against 5.47 extrinsic, F(1, 894) = 12.56, p < .01. Asian managers rated the two alike, 7.29 and 7.24, F(1, 188) = 2.54, not significant. Latin American managers judged their employees more intrinsically than extrinsically motivated, 7.01 against 5.78, F(1, 265) = 5.85, p < .05, which matched what those employees said about themselves. Woolley and Fishbach ran five studies with 1,428 people on items modified from Heath. In their third study, 208 online participants either predicted what recruiters care about or reported what they themselves cared about as recruiters. Recruiters valued intrinsic rewards at 1.86 on a scale running from -3 to 3, above the 1.31 that candidates predicted, F(1, 206) = 14.91, p < .001, partial eta squared .07. The prediction for extrinsic rewards was accurate, F(1, 206) = 1.87, p = .173. In that test the gap sat on the intrinsic side alone.

study.cite: DeVoe, S. E., & Iyengar, S. S. (2004). Managers' theories of subordinates: A cross-cultural examination of manager perceptions of motivation and appraisal of performance. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 93(1), 47-61.

limits: No preregistered direct replication of Heath's studies was found. The search covered Crossref, PubMed, the papers Semantic Scholar lists as citing Heath, and general web search. Heath's own paper is paywalled, so every figure attributed to it here arrives through DeVoe and Iyengar. DeVoe and Iyengar compared managers' ratings of their employees with those employees' self-ratings, which is not the within-person self-other comparison Heath ran. The bias is defined against self-reports as the standard of truth, and Rynes, Gerhart and Minette argue that self-reports understate how much pay drives behaviour. They set survey rankings beside behavioural evidence, including Judiesch's meta-analysis in which individual pay incentives raised productivity by 43.7% on average. If self-ranking of pay is depressed by social desirability, part of the gap belongs to the self side rather than to the prediction side. The pattern predates Heath and appears in a different format. Jurgensen's thirty-year study of 57,000 job applicants ranked ten job attributes, and on Rynes and colleagues' account pay came fifth for men and seventh for women in their own preferences, and first for both when the same list was ranked for someone just like themselves.
misreadings: This is not the overjustification effect. That claim is about what a promised reward does to later behaviour; this one is about what people believe of other people's motives, and it predicts nothing about whether an incentive will work. It is also not Miller and Ratner's finding on self-interest. Their five studies had participants overestimating what a financial reward would do to peers' willingness to donate blood, and overestimating what group membership would do to peers' attitudes, with that tendency largely unrelated to the pull self-interest exerted on the participants themselves. Heath's abstract states that the extrinsic incentives bias is separable from a self-serving bias and runs against the actor-observer effect, so it is not a special case of either. Nothing here shows that pay fails to motivate. Woolley and Fishbach raise the bias in their 2015 paper and argue against it as the explanation of their own result, which is that people value intrinsic incentives more while doing an activity than before or after it, whereas extrinsic incentives are valued about the same either way. A self-directed version of the question gives a related answer without being the same claim. Kuratomi and colleagues ran seven experiments in which people worked on long repetitive tasks, and participants were engaged more than they had predicted. In their flanker experiment with 80 UK adults, predicted engagement was 3.26 against actual 3.79, F(1, 76) = 13.09, p < .001, and the Prediction by Reward interaction reached F(1, 76) = 7.99, p < .01, with the shortfall gone once performance-based money was on offer.
